questions.prompt: When must you have proof of insurance with you?
choices: Whenever you drive.
Only after you have been in a collision.
When you renew registration, not day to day.
questions.explanation: You must carry proof of financial responsibility (insurance) whenever you drive, including for a drive test.

questions.prompt: After a collision, what must you show the other driver?
choices: Only your name and phone number, nothing else.
Nothing, unless the police come to the scene.
License, registration, insurance, and address.
questions.explanation: Show your license, registration card, insurance information and current address to the other driver, police and anyone else involved.

questions.prompt: What is the least your insurance may cover for the death or injury of one person?
questions.explanation: Minimum coverage is $30,000 for one person's death or injury, $60,000 for more than one person, and $15,000 for property damage.

questions.prompt: What is the least your insurance may cover for the death or injury of more than one person?
questions.explanation: Minimum coverage is $60,000 for death or injury to more than one person.

questions.prompt: What is the least your insurance may cover for property damage?
questions.explanation: Minimum coverage for property damage is $15,000.

questions.prompt: Before buying car insurance, what should you check?
choices: The agent has been approved by the DMV.
The agent has an office in your own city.
The agent is licensed by the Department of Insurance.
questions.explanation: Make sure the agent, broker or provider is licensed by the California Department of Insurance.

questions.prompt: You are in a collision without insurance, and it was not your fault. What can happen?
choices: A suspension of up to four years.
Nothing, since you weren't at fault.
A fine, with no license suspension.
questions.explanation: Without proper insurance, your driving privilege will be suspended for up to four years no matter who was at fault.

questions.prompt: You see a car's emergency flashers on the road ahead. What should you do?
choices: Keep your speed and change lanes fast.
Stop behind it until it moves.
Slow down and pass with care.
questions.explanation: Flashers may mean a collision or other emergency ahead. Slow down and pass carefully.

questions.prompt: You bump another car in slow traffic and see no damage. What must you do?
choices: Keep going, since nothing was damaged.
Stop; driving off would be a hit-and-run.
Wave, and drive on if the driver waves back.
questions.explanation: If you are in a collision you must stop. Leaving the scene is a hit-and-run, which is punished severely.

questions.prompt: After a minor collision, no one is hurt and both cars still run. What should you do?
choices: Move out of traffic, then call 911.
Leave the cars where they are for police.
Drive home and call the other driver later.
questions.explanation: If no one is hurt, move your vehicle out of traffic and then call 911. If anyone is hurt, call 911 right away.

questions.prompt: Someone was injured in your collision. How soon must it be reported to law enforcement?
choices: Within 24 hours.
Within 10 days.
Within 72 hours.
questions.explanation: Report injury or fatal collisions to law enforcement within 24 hours. The 10-day deadline is for the DMV report.

questions.prompt: You hit a parked car and can't find the owner. What must you do?
choices: Leave a note and report it to police.
Leave, since you tried to find them.
Leave a note, with no need to report it.
questions.explanation: Securely attach a note with your name, phone number and address, and report the collision to law enforcement.

questions.prompt: You hit a deer and it is injured. What should you do?
choices: Call the humane society or police.
Move it off the road yourself.
Drive on; animals aren't reportable.
questions.explanation: Call the nearest humane society or law enforcement, and don't try to move an injured animal.

questions.prompt: Someone had a minor injury in your collision. What is the deadline for reporting it to the DMV?
choices: 10 days.
24 hours.
30 days.
questions.explanation: Report to the DMV within 10 days if anyone was hurt, even slightly, or if damage was over $1,000. Police must be told within 24 hours of an injury.

questions.prompt: Your collision caused $2,000 in damage, and the other driver was at fault. Who must file an SR 1 with the DMV?
choices: Each driver, at fault or not.
Only the driver at fault.
The officer at the scene.
questions.explanation: Each driver must file an SR 1, whether or not they caused the collision. Law enforcement will not make the report for you.

questions.prompt: What happens if you don't file a required SR 1 collision report?
choices: The police will file it for you.
Your license will be suspended.
Your insurer files it for a fee.
questions.explanation: Your driving privilege will be suspended if you fail to file a required report, and law enforcement will not file it for you.
